1079.title: We did it ourselves
1079.hook: the best leaders are barely noticed, and people say "we did it ourselves" (Tao Te Ching 17)
1079.howItsDone: Some teachers, parents and managers who read the Tao Te Ching take chapter seventeen as a model: they help quietly and step back, so the people they help can own the result.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was return to the root: what rises goes back, and the going back is stillness. That was your line too.

A kid is learning to ride a bike. A parent runs alongside, one hand on the back of the seat, steadying it. Then, without saying anything, the parent lets go. The kid keeps pedaling, wobbles, steadies, and rides to the end of the street alone, then turns around, beaming: I did it! And the parent, out of breath, says: you did. Not a word about the hand on the seat. Chapter seventeen of the Tao Te Ching says that moment is what the best kind of leading looks like.
screen: `A HAND ON THE BACK OF THE SEAT.` → `THE PARENT LETS GO.` → `I DID IT!`

segments.voice: First, a ladder of leaders. With the best, the chapter says, people barely know they're there. Next, people love and praise them. Next, people fear them. And at the bottom, people mock them. Love and praise land second, not first: a leader everyone praises is still standing in the center of the picture. The best one has stepped out of it. Second, trust. A short, sharp line: where there isn't enough trust, there will be no trust in return. A leader who doesn't trust people breeds people who don't trust the leader. The best leader steps back partly because they trust the people to do the work. Third, the quiet hand. The best leaders are unhurried and careful with their words. They do what's needed, without speeches, and go quiet again. Fourth, the ending that names today's lesson. When the work is done and things turn out well, the people all say: this happened by itself; we did it ourselves. The word underneath is ziran: of itself so, or natural. The chapter counts it as success when nobody gives the leader the credit. That can be hard to want. But a parent, a teacher, a manager, a friend, anyone who has helped someone grow, has had the chance to be that hand on the seat: steadying, then letting go, and letting the joy belong to someone else.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you could help, a coworker stuck on something, a kid with homework, a friend making a decision, and picture helping in a way that leaves them holding the result: a question instead of an answer, a hand on the seat, then letting go. Notice whether part of you wants them to know it was you; that's all right, so just notice it and let it rest.
We did it ourselves. Chapter seventeen's sign of the best leading: the work gets done, and the people say it happened of itself. Today's word.
Your line: they did it themselves. The joy of the ride belongs to the rider. See you tomorrow.

1080.title: When the way is lost
1080.hook: when the great Tao is forgotten, rules about kindness and duty appear (Tao Te Ching 18)
1080.howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching use chapter eighteen as a check on themselves: they notice when they do good only because a rule says so, and look for kindness that comes before any rule.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was we did it ourselves: the best leaders go barely noticed. Your line was they did it themselves.

A sign taped to an office fridge: please label your food. Below it, a second sign: please don't take food that isn't yours. Below that, in red: whoever is eating my yogurt, stop. Nobody wrote those signs on day one. On day one, people just didn't take each other's lunches. Each sign marks the spot where something was already lost. Chapter eighteen of the Tao Te Ching is only a few lines long, and it reads every sign like that one.
screen: `PLEASE LABEL YOUR FOOD.` → `WHOEVER IS EATING MY YOGURT, STOP.` → `EACH SIGN MARKS A LOSS.`

segments.voice: First, the opening line. When the great Way is abandoned, the chapter says, kindness and righteousness appear. That sounds backward. Aren't those good things? They are. The point is about when people start talking about them. On this reading, no one needs speeches about kindness where kindness is simply how things are; the speeches start once it's gone missing. Second, the pattern repeats. When cleverness and know-how show up, great pretending follows. When families fall out of harmony, people start praising devoted children and loving parents. When a country falls into disorder, loyal ministers get noticed. Each virtue becomes visible, and gets a name and a rule, at the moment its absence is felt. Third, who's listening. Kindness and righteousness, ren and yi, are words the school of Confucius treasured, and some readers hear this chapter as part of a conversation between the two schools. Confucian teachers have their own answer: that naming and practicing virtue is how people grow into it. The Tao Te Ching's line is that the naming comes late. Fourth, the hint inside. If rules about kindness are a sign the way was lost, the way itself is something before the rule. Not unkindness, and not a world without rules: a kindness that came first, before anyone needed to write it on the fridge. The chapter leaves a question: can a person find their way back to that, one small act at a time?

segments.voice: Think of one small kindness you could do that no rule asks of you, not because it's polite or someone's watching, just because it fits: refilling the coffee pot, holding a door a little longer, a message to someone who's been quiet. Hold that one act in mind, and notice whether it feels different from the ones you do because you're supposed to.
When the way is lost. Chapter eighteen's warning: the rules about kindness and duty show up after the thing they describe has gone missing. Today's word.

1081.title: Plain silk, uncarved wood
1081.hook: show plainness, embrace simplicity, have few desires (Tao Te Ching 19)
1081.howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching take pu, the uncarved block, as a reason to keep their lives and belongings plain, and to leave room in themselves for what isn't finished yet.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was when the way is lost: rules about kindness come after the way goes missing. Your line was before the rule.

Two pieces of wood on a workbench. One is a finished carving: a bird, every feather cut in, polished, perfect. The other is a plain block, straight from the tree, nothing done to it yet. Which one could still become anything? The bird is beautiful, and it will only ever be a bird. The block could be a bowl, a spoon, a bird, a handle, a toy. Chapter nineteen of the Tao Te Ching reaches for that block. Its name for it is a single word, pu.
screen: `A FINISHED CARVING.` → `A PLAIN BLOCK.` → `WHICH COULD STILL BECOME ANYTHING?`

segments.voice: First, the chapter starts by throwing things out. Give up sageliness and cleverness, it says, and the people will be better off. Give up kindness and righteousness, and the people will return to devotion and care in their families. Give up craftiness and profit, and there'll be no thieves. It picks up where yesterday left off: the named virtues came after the way was lost, so let the names go. Second, it admits that's not enough. Throwing things out leaves a hole, and people need something to hold on to. So it offers three things: show plainness, embrace the uncarved, be less selfish and want less. Third, the two pictures. Plainness here is su, raw silk, undyed, the cloth before anyone colors it. The uncarved is pu, wood in the block, before anyone shapes it. Both are materials in their first state: not poor, not ugly, just not yet worked over. A person, like silk or wood, can be dyed and carved by praise, ambition, cleverness and wanting, until there's no room left to become anything else. Fourth, what it isn't. Pu isn't a call to be simple-minded. Some readers hear an invitation to stay a little unfinished, to keep some of yourself raw and plain, with room to grow in a new direction. The carving is admired. The block is free.

segments.voice: Rest your eyes on one plain thing near you, a cotton shirt, a wooden spoon, a white mug, a glass of water, and notice it as it is, with nothing added: its weight, its color, its texture. Then turn the same attention to yourself, the part of you before titles and opinions and plans: not better, not worse, just plain and uncarved.
Pu. Uncarved wood, the block before anyone shapes it: chapter nineteen's picture of a person not yet worked over. Today's word.
Your line: uncarved. The block can still become a bowl, a spoon or a bird. Same time tomorrow.

1082.title: Drifting like an infant
1082.hook: others are busy and bright; I alone drift, like a baby not yet smiling (Tao Te Ching 20)
1082.howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter twenty as permission to do nothing for a while: a stretch of unscheduled time, with no goal, when they are not trying to keep up with anyone.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was pu, the uncarved block: plain wood and plain silk, left as they are. Your line was uncarved. Today the book speaks in the first person.

The square is full. Music, lanterns, food going around on platters, people calling to each other across the crowd. Everyone has somewhere to be and something to say. Off to one side, a single person stands still. Not sulking, not judging. Just not swept up. Ask what they're doing, and the honest answer is nothing much. Chapter twenty of the Tao Te Ching is spoken by that person. It says I, and the I sounds a little lonely, and a little free.
screen: `A FULL SQUARE.` → `ONE PERSON STANDS STILL.` → `CHAPTER TWENTY SAYS I.`

segments.voice: First, the crowd at the feast. The chapter describes the people around the speaker as bright and pleased, as if at a great banquet, or climbing a terrace in spring. Nothing in the text says they are wicked. They are simply full, busy, sure of what they're doing. Second, I alone, adrift. Against that brightness the speaker sets himself. Others have more than enough; he seems to have lost something. Others are sharp and clear; he seems dull and murky, restless as the sea, blown about like a wind with nowhere to stop. It reads like a confession of failure, and some readers think it's meant to sound that way, a little wry, a little sad. Third, an infant not yet smiling. Then the picture at the center. In Legge's translation: "I am like an infant which has not yet smiled." A newborn hasn't started performing. It hasn't learned to smile on cue, to look interested, to keep up. It just drifts, taking everything in. The speaker has stayed, or gone back, to that early place, before the social face goes on. Fourth, fed by the mother. The chapter ends by naming what sets the speaker apart: he values being fed by the mother. Some readers take the mother to be the Tao itself, the source this book keeps returning to. So the drifting isn't aimless after all. It's a person who stopped grabbing at the banquet because they are already being fed.
screen: `THE CROWD AT THE FEAST.` · `I ALONE, ADRIFT.` · `AN INFANT NOT YET SMILING.` · `FED BY THE MOTHER.` · then, large: `I AM LIKE AN INFANT.`

segments.voice: Be unbusy for a moment: don't meditate, and don't improve anything. Let your face go slack, the way a face looks before anyone is watching, and let your eyes rest on whatever is in front of them without naming it. If a task tugs at you, let it tug, and stay where you are, at the edge of the square.
Drifting like an infant. Chapter twenty's picture of someone not swept up by the crowd, unperformed, still being fed by the source. Today's word.
Your line: drifting. Under the ready smile and the busy look, there's a face that doesn't have to perform. See you tomorrow.

1083.title: Elusive and real
1083.hook: the Tao is shadowy and elusive, yet within it is something real (Tao Te Ching 21)
1083.howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching sit with chapter twenty-one's paradox: the Way can't be grasped or seen, yet the text insists there is something real and trustworthy within it.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was drifting like an infant: standing apart from the busy crowd, unperformed, still fed by the source. Your line was drifting.

The wind can't be held in a hand. What you get is the evidence: a flag snapping on a pole, a field of grass bending all one way, a door that slams on its own. You can't point at the thing itself, and yet nobody standing in a gale thinks it's imaginary. Some solid things in a life work like that: trust between two old friends, the pull of a place you grew up. Hard to pin down, and hard to doubt. Chapter twenty-one of the Tao Te Ching describes the Way in exactly that double sense.
screen: `NOBODY HOLDS THE WIND.` → `ONLY THE EVIDENCE.` → `HARD TO PIN, HARD TO DOUBT.`

segments.voice: First, virtue follows the Way. The chapter opens by saying that the shape of great virtue comes from following the Tao, and the Tao alone. Whatever goodness looks like, its source is this thing the chapter is about to describe. Second, shadowy and elusive. The description is slippery on purpose. The Chinese uses a pair of words, huang and hu, that suggest something dim, flickering, glimpsed out of the corner of an eye. You look, and it slips out of sight. You reach, and it isn't where your hand lands. Third, something real inside. Then the turn. Within that dimness, the chapter says, there are forms. Within it, there are things. Deep and dark as it is, there is an essence in it, and that essence is very real. There is even something trustworthy in it, a kind of proof. Elusive is not the same as empty. Fourth, how do I know? By this. The chapter ends with the speaker asking how he knows the way all things began. His answer is two words: by this. No argument. He points at what's in front of him, the world as it is, as if the evidence were the flag and the grass. Some readers hear a quiet confidence in that: you can't hold the Way, but you can live in its weather.
screen: `VIRTUE FOLLOWS THE WAY.` · `SHADOWY AND ELUSIVE.` · `SOMETHING REAL INSIDE.` · `HOW DO I KNOW? BY THIS.` · then, large: `ELUSIVE, AND REAL.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you rely on without being able to show it to anyone: that a certain person means well, that rest will help, that morning will come. Don't defend it; just lean on it for a minute, the way you'd lean on a wall you can't see in the dark. If you pray, this may be a place for that; if you don't, the leaning is enough.
Elusive and real. Chapter twenty-one's picture of the Way: dim and slippery to the hand, with something true and trustworthy at its center. Today's word.
Your line: something real. Hard to measure is not the same as unreal. Rest well.

1084.title: Yield and be whole
1084.hook: bend and be straight, empty and be full (Tao Te Ching 22)
1084.howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching treat chapter twenty-two as a habit for daily life: giving way on small disagreements rather than pressing to win them.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was elusive and real: the Way, dim and slippery, with something true inside. Your line was something real.

A couch is stuck in a doorway. One person is in the hall, shoving. The other is inside the room, pulling. The couch doesn't move, and both of them are getting louder. Then a neighbor wanders past, looks for a second, and says, tilt it. Stand it on its end, turn it a little. The couch slides through as if the doorway had grown. Nobody got stronger. Somebody gave up the straight line. Chapter twenty-two of the Tao Te Ching is built on that moment, when bending is what gets the thing through.
screen: `A COUCH IN A DOORWAY.` → `SHOVE, PULL, NOTHING.` → `TILT IT.`

segments.voice: First, bent, then whole. The chapter opens with a run of reversals. In Legge's translation: "The partial becomes complete; the crooked, straight; the empty, full; the worn out, new." Each pair goes against common sense. We expect the bent thing to break. The chapter says the bent thing is the one that stays whole. Second, empty, then full. A cup that's already full can't receive; only an empty one can be filled. What is worn out makes room for what is new. Wanting follows the same pattern: whoever wants little, it says, gets it, and whoever wants a lot gets lost. Third, the sage doesn't push. Then the chapter turns to a person. The sage doesn't put himself on display, and so he shines. He doesn't insist he's right, and so he stands out. He doesn't boast, and so his work counts. He isn't proud of himself, and so he lasts. Fourth, no one can contend. Because the sage doesn't contend with anyone, the chapter says, no one in the world can contend with him. There's nothing to push against. It closes by asking whether the old saying about the bent being made whole was just empty words. Its answer: no. Becoming whole really comes this way. Yielding here isn't losing. It's how the couch gets through the door.

Yield and be whole. Chapter twenty-two's run of reversals: the bent made whole, the empty filled, and the one who doesn't contend, whom no one can contend with. Today's word.

1085.title: The whirlwind
1085.hook: a whirlwind doesn't last all morning; speak little (Tao Te Ching 23)
1085.howItsDone: Some people who read the Tao Te Ching take chapter twenty-three as a practice of restraint in speech: saying what is needed, then stopping, and letting strong feelings pass before they talk.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was yield and be whole: the bent made whole, and the one who doesn't contend. Your line was yield and be whole.

The sky goes green-gray in the middle of the afternoon. Wind tears through the street, a trash can rolls past on its side, rain comes down so hard it bounces. Everyone ducks into doorways. And then, almost before the shirts are soaked, it's over. The sun is out, and someone is already wiping off a café chair. While a storm like that is happening, it can seem as if it will never stop. It does. Chapter twenty-three of the Tao Te Ching watches one blow through, and draws a lesson about how much we say.
screen: `THE SKY GOES GREEN-GRAY.` → `EVERYONE DUCKS.` → `THEN IT'S OVER.`

segments.voice: First, speak little, like nature. The chapter opens with just a few characters that link saying little with what is so of itself, the natural way of things. Nature doesn't talk much. It doesn't explain itself. Second, no storm lasts all morning. In Legge's translation: "A violent wind does not last for a whole morning; a sudden rain does not last for the whole day." Who makes the wind and the rain? Heaven and earth, the chapter says. And if even heaven and earth can't keep up a burst like that for long, how much less can a person. A rant, a lecture, a flood of messages late at night: loud and fast runs out. Third, you become what you follow. Whoever follows the Way becomes one with the Way. Whoever follows virtue becomes one with virtue. And whoever follows loss becomes one with loss. What you keep company with, you turn into, and the Way, it adds, is glad to have you. Fourth, trust that isn't enough. The chapter closes with a line the book used before, in chapter seventeen: where trust falls short, there is no trust in return. Too many words can be a sign of that. People who trust each other don't need to keep talking. And this closes a week: leaders whose people said we did it ourselves, the way lost, the uncarved block, drifting like an infant, the elusive and real, yielding to be whole, and now the whirlwind.
screen: `SPEAK LITTLE, LIKE NATURE.` · `NO STORM LASTS ALL MORNING.` · `YOU BECOME WHAT YOU FOLLOW.` · `TRUST THAT ISN'T ENOUGH.` · then, large: `A VIOLENT WIND DOES NOT LAST.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you need to say to someone: a request, an answer, an apology, a no. Say it silently the long way, with every reason and softener, then again in half the words, then once more with only what's needed. Sit in the quiet after that last, plain version, and let it be enough.
The whirlwind. Chapter twenty-three's violent wind that can't last a whole morning, and its advice to say little, the way nature does. Today's word.
Your line: speak little. Storms blow over, and so do floods of words. That's the week.
